study.title: Psalm 85 Restoration, peace, and justice that precede the Lord
study.overview: The psalm recalls the restoration already received by God, but does not treat this as the final point: the people still live under signs of divine discipline and cry out for complete renewal. Prayer is born out of the memory of past mercies and advances to a broader hope, in which goodness, truth, justice and peace do not appear separated, but gathered in the saving action of the Lord. The closure of the psalm presents God coming to meet a people who want to return to the path of their steps, that is, to live under the practical direction of divine justice.

outline.title: Memories of Restoration and Forgiveness
outline.explanation: The psalmist begins by remembering that the LORD was favorable to the land, restored the people and forgave his guilt. This memory is not only informative; it nourishes the confidence that God has acted before and therefore can act again. The relief of punishment is presented as the direct fruit of divine forgiveness.

outline.title: Request for renewal and peace response
outline.explanation: The community asks God to interrupt his wrath, revive the people and grant salvation. The psalmist then takes the position of those who listen, showing that true prayer also includes silence and waits for the word of God. The expected response is peace, reserved to those who fear him and do not return to folly.

outline.title: The harmony of salvation and the way of righteousness
outline.explanation: The final part poetically describes salvation as the encounter of goodness, truth, justice, and peace. The earth again bears fruit, a visible sign of restored blessing. The psalm ends with justice going before the Lord himself, as if he prepared the way for his presence among his people.

study.context: The notes provided indicate that this psalm is often understood as linked to the period after the return of the people of Judah from exile in Babylon, when the community still perceived signs of God's displeasure and prayed for fuller restoration. This reading appears in more than one commentator, but should be treated as a probable interpretation, not as explicitly stated by the biblical text itself.
study.theology: The psalm unites three central ideas. First, God's forgiveness is the basis of the restoration of the people: guilt is not ignored, but covered and removed by divine action. Second, salvation is not only individual; it involves collective life, the earth, public peace, and the return of glory among the people. Third, true moral and spiritual restoration appears when justice and peace walk together. This avoids separating holiness from reconciliation: in the psalm, God not only delivers from judgment, but forms a people who walk back in their ways. The righteousness that goes before him suggests that the presence of the Lord is not neutral; it orders life, corrects the course and prepares the people to receive it.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm describes renewal as a scenario in which love, truth, justice and peace unite and transform the created order.
The psalmist, after praying, puts himself in a listening attitude and awaits a peace response from God.
The righteousness that goes forth of the Lord is understood as something that prepares the way for his coming and guides the sinner to his footsteps.

questions: What signs of restoration have we have received from God, but we still need to ask him to complete in us and among us?
In practice, how can we hear God more reverently, rather than speaking only amid anxiety?
How can justice and peace be sought together in the life of the church, family and public witness?
study.practice: Pray with memory and hope: start by thanking the mercies already received, confess the need for renewal and then stay silent to hear the direction of God. Practice concrete reconciliation also: where there is a break, seek to act with truth and justice, without abandoning peace. In addition, observe community life and ask the Lord to make fruitful what today seems arid, remembering that his blessing also reaches the visible daily life.
study.uncertainty: The notes suggest, but do not definitively prove, that the psalm was composed after the return of exile. There are also Christian readings that relate the final verse to the coming of Christ; this appears in the notes as theological interpretation, not as an explicit statement of the original text. The poetic expressions of justice, truth, and peace should be read as inspired images, not as technical or chronological descriptions.
